titulo: Querer, poder, deber and tener que: Deber, tener que, hay que and other stem-changing verbs

aula.titulo: Querer, poder, deber and tener que
aula.objetivo: Say what you want, can and should do with querer, poder, deber, tener que and hay que; understand stem-changing verbs (e → ie, o → ue); ask for permission, make requests, and decline politely.

sessao.titulo: Deber, tener que, hay que and other stem-changing verbs

blocos.titulo: Deber, tener que, hay que, and the «boot» in other verbs
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: «deber» (should, ought to) is regular: debo, debes, debe, debemos, debéis, deben. The infinitive follows it: «Debes dormir más» (it's advisable). STEP 2: «tener que» + infinitive is a concrete obligation or need: «Tengo que trabajar hoy». «Tener» has «tengo» and changes e → ie: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen. It's always written with «que»; «tener de» doesn't exist. STEP 3: «hay que» + infinitive is a general obligation, with no subject: «Hay que pagar en la caja». The form «hay» never changes. STEP 4: a rule of thumb: «debo» for moral duty or advice, «tengo que» for what circumstances require of you specifically, «hay que» for what applies to everyone. STEP 5: the vowel change you saw in «querer» and «poder» shows up in many other verbs, with the same boot shape: e → ie (empezar: empiezo; pensar: pienso; preferir: prefiero; entender: entiendo), o → ue (volver: vuelvo; dormir: duermo; encontrar: encuentro; costar: cuesta), and u → ue (jugar: juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan). STEP 6: use them with these structures: «empezar a + infinitive» (to start doing something), «pensar + infinitive» (to intend to), «volver a + infinitive» (to do again), «preferir + infinitive», «jugar al + sport» (jugar al fútbol, al tenis). STEP 7: not every verb changes its vowel. «Comer», «vivir», «hablar» and «salir» don't change; you'll pick up the list of verbs that do, little by little. When in doubt, listen for it — it's what the dictionary flags with «(ie)» or «(ue)».
blocos.comparacao: English has nothing like this vowel-swap pattern — «I start, I think, I prefer, I sleep, I play» stay exactly the same in every form — so the «boot» shape is new grammar to learn rather than something transferable. «Tener que» maps closely onto English «have to», and «hay que» onto the impersonal «one has to / it's necessary to», with no subject attached either way.

exemplos.ru: La clase empieza a las nueve.

exemplos.pt: I'm thinking of traveling in August.

erros.errado: [misto] Empezo a trabajar a las ocho.
erros.certo: [misto] Empiezo a trabajar a las ocho.

erros.motivo: «Hay que» is impersonal and has no subject.

blocos.enunciado: Say out loud what you have to do this week (three sentences with «tengo que»), what you should do for your health (two with «debo»), and what you prefer to do in your free time (two with «prefiero»).
Conjugate «querer» and «poder» from memory. Then ask a friend three things out loud with «¿Puedes…?» and a stranger with «¿Puede…?».
